newsitem.title: UK: EU sees trouble ahead on airport runway slot rules.
newsitem.headline: EU sees trouble ahead on airport runway slot rules.

text.p: The European Union is unlikely to make new rules this year on the way takeoff and landing time "slots" are distributed, and possibly traded, at Europe's busiest airports, a senior EU official said on Tuesday.
The European Commission's head of air transport policy, Frederik Sorensen, told Reuters the Commission intends to make its final proposals next month.
But he said member states were so divided in their views over how the rules should be amended that no change would be made this year.
"It is unlikely that there would be any decision by the Council (of Ministers) before December," he said.

He told an industry conference earlier that the Commission was assessing several options, including the idea of formally allowing airlines to trade slots at congested airports such as London Heathrow, but all options faced some opposition.

"I can only say that when the Commission puts forward any proposal in this respect, it is going to have a very complicated passage through the Council of Ministers of member states," he told a conference on Slots and Access to Airport Facilities at the Royal Aeronautical Society in London.
"I don't see that there is any so-called qualified majority (backing) for any of the options," he added.

The Commission announced last year it wanted to change the rules to free up the way slots are allocated and exchanged to give new competition a better chance of gaining access to the most congested airports, where established airlines can retain slot times in perpetuity under so-called "grandfather rights".
In particular it said it was looking at the idea of allowing secondary trading in slots.
Sorensen told Reuters on Tuesday that this proposal currently only had the backing of five member states but the Commission was still looking for a trading mechanism.

"Some sort of mechanism which is dependent on market forces," he had told the conference. "If you ask who should have access to scarce resources, my reaction as an economist is to say you should pay for what you want," he said.

Airline executives say a single pair of daily takeoff and landing slots at Heathrow, Europe's biggest airport, could change hands for as much as three million pounds if a public market was established.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert told Britain this month that Heathrow's biggest user, British Airways, was banned by current EU rules from selling slots it has been asked to give up as a condition for approving its proposed alliance with American Airlines.

But legal experts said on Tuesday that the meaning of the current rules as encoded by Regulation 95/93 Article 8 was so uncertain that on any legal interpretation it probably allows trading, if only by omission.
"It (the regulation) is ambiguous where it's specific and generally speaking it's vague," said barrister Robert Webb QC.
"The Commission don't like it (slot trading) but under the present regulation I do not see why not," he told the conference.
"It completely fails to address the issue of monetary payment," said another conference speaker, aviation law specialist Hugh O'Donovan of solicitors Wilde Sapte.
"I would have thought monetary payment is not illegal in the absence of an express provision...It is not enough to say something is not in the spirit of a (EU) regulation."
